items.title: AI ENGINEERING ROADMAP
items.summary:
AI ENGINEERING ROADMAP
│
├── 0. Engineering Foundations (don't over-invest)
│   ├── Python done properly (type hints, async/await, Pydantic, uv)
│   ├── Git, Linux shell, Docker basics
│   ├── HTTP, REST, JSON, building APIs with FastAPI
│   ├── SQL + Postgres
│   ├── Math intuition only
│   │   ├── Vectors, dot products, matrix multiplication
│   │   ├── Probability & sampling
│   │   └── Derivatives & gradients
│   └── ★ Build: FastAPI + Postgres service, running in Docker
│
├── 1. ML Foundations (just enough)
│   ├── The training loop: data → model → loss → optimizer
│   ├── Train / validation / test splits, overfitting
│   ├── Metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1
│   ├── Gradient descent & backprop (do one by hand)
│   ├── PyTorch: tensors, autograd, writing a training loop
│   ├── Embeddings as a concept
│   └── ★ Build: train a small text classifier in PyTorch
│
├── 2. How LLMs Actually Work
│   ├── Tokenization (BPE) and why tokens ≠ words
│   ├── Attention & the transformer block
│   ├── Next-token prediction & sampling (temperature, top-p)
│   ├── Pretraining → SFT → RLHF / RL with verifiable rewards
│   ├── Context windows & the KV cache (why long context costs more)
│   ├── Reasoning models & test-time compute
│   ├── Why models hallucinate
│   └── ★ Build: a tiny GPT from scratch (nanoGPT-style)
│
├── 3. Building with Model APIs
│   ├── Messages, roles & system prompts
│   ├── Streaming
│   ├── Structured outputs (JSON schema → typed objects)
│   ├── Tool use / function calling
│   ├── Multimodal input (images, PDFs, audio)
│   ├── Prompt caching & batch APIs
│   ├── Token, cost & latency math
│   ├── Retries, timeouts, rate limits
│   ├── Choosing a model: frontier vs small vs open-weight
│   └── ★ Build: streaming CLI assistant with 2 tools and typed output
│
├── 4. Prompt & Context Engineering
│   ├── Clear instructions, examples, structured prompts
│   ├── Context engineering: what goes in the window, and why
│   ├── Letting the model think (reasoning, scratchpads)
│   ├── Prompt chaining & task decomposition
│   ├── Prompts as versioned code
│   └── ★ Build: 3 prompt versions for one task, compared on 30 test cases
│
├── 5. Evals (the skill that matters most)
│   ├── Why vibe-checking stops scaling
│   ├── Error analysis: read traces, label failure types
│   ├── Golden datasets built from real failures
│   ├── Code-based checks (schemas, assertions, exact match)
│   ├── LLM-as-judge, validated against human labels
│   ├── Pairwise comparisons
│   ├── Offline vs online evals
│   ├── Evals in CI as regression tests
│   └── ★ Build: eval harness for your phase 3 project; prove a change helped
│
│   ◆ CHECKPOINT 25: you can ship an LLM feature and measure it
│
├── 6. Retrieval & RAG
│   ├── When RAG beats long context (and when it doesn't)
│   ├── Embeddings & similarity search
│   ├── Chunking strategies
│   ├── pgvector first; a dedicated vector DB only when needed
│   ├── Hybrid search (BM25 + vectors) & reranking
│   ├── Query rewriting
│   ├── Retrieval evals (recall@k, MRR), separate from answer evals
│   ├── Citations & grounding
│   └── ★ Build: Q&A over a real document set, with citations and retrieval metrics
│
├── 7. Agents
│   ├── What an agent is: model + tools + loop
│   ├── Workflows vs agents (use a workflow when you can)
│   ├── Patterns
│   │   ├── Routing
│   │   ├── Parallelization
│   │   ├── Orchestrator–workers
│   │   └── Evaluator–optimizer
│   ├── Tool design (names, descriptions, error messages)
│   ├── Memory: in-context vs long-term stores
│   ├── Long tasks: compaction & sub-agents
│   ├── MCP (Model Context Protocol)
│   ├── Coding agents & computer use
│   ├── Multi-agent: when it helps vs when it just burns tokens
│   ├── Human-in-the-loop & permissions
│   ├── Agent evals: trajectory vs outcome
│   └── ★ Build: an agent with raw API calls, then rebuild it in one framework and compare
│
│   ◆ CHECKPOINT 50: you can build RAG and agents and prove they work
│
├── 8. Production AI (LLMOps)
│   ├── Serving: FastAPI + streaming to a frontend (SSE)
│   ├── Tracing & observability (OpenTelemetry + an LLM tracing tool)
│   ├── Caching (exact & semantic) and cost controls
│   ├── Model routing & fallbacks
│   ├── Latency: streaming, parallel calls, smaller models
│   ├── Guardrails: input/output validation, PII handling
│   ├── A/B testing prompts and models
│   ├── Feedback loop: user signals → dataset → evals
│   └── ★ Build: deploy your RAG app or agent with tracing, cost tracking and CI evals
│
├── 9. AI Security
│   ├── Prompt injection (direct & indirect)
│   ├── Data exfiltration through tools
│   ├── Least privilege & sandboxing for tools
│   ├── Jailbreaks & output filtering
│   ├── OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
│   └── ★ Build: red-team your own agent and fix what breaks
│
├── 10. Open Models & Inference
│   ├── The open-weight ecosystem
│   ├── Hugging Face Transformers
│   ├── Running locally (Ollama, llama.cpp)
│   ├── Quantization (int8 / int4, GGUF, AWQ)
│   ├── Serving at scale: vLLM / SGLang, continuous batching, PagedAttention
│   ├── GPU memory math (weights + KV cache)
│   ├── Throughput vs latency trade-offs
│   └── ★ Build: serve an open model with vLLM and benchmark tokens/sec
│
│   ◆ CHECKPOINT 75: you can run, secure and self-host AI in production
│
├── 11. Fine-tuning & Post-training
│   ├── When to fine-tune (after prompting + RAG plateau, not before)
│   ├── Dataset creation & synthetic data
│   ├── SFT with LoRA / QLoRA
│   ├── Preference tuning (DPO)
│   ├── RL for LLMs: GRPO, verifiable rewards, RL environments
│   ├── Distillation: big model → small model
│   ├── Comparing against the prompted baseline
│   └── ★ Build: LoRA-tune a small model that beats a prompted one on cost or latency
│
├── 12. AI System Design
│   ├── Requirements → model choice → eval plan → architecture
│   ├── The quality / cost / latency triangle
│   ├── Build vs buy, API vs self-host
│   ├── Case studies
│   │   ├── Customer support agent
│   │   ├── RAG over company documents
│   │   ├── Coding assistant
│   │   ├── AI search engine (Perplexity-style)
│   │   ├── Voice agent
│   │   ├── Document extraction pipeline
│   │   └── LLM gateway for a company
│   └── ★ Build: written design docs for 3 case studies
│
├── 13. Specialize (pick 1–2)
│   ├── Agents & agent infrastructure
│   ├── Coding agents & dev tools
│   ├── Voice & realtime (STT → LLM → TTS)
│   ├── Multimodal & vision-language
│   ├── Document AI (OCR, extraction)
│   ├── Search & recommendations with embeddings
│   └── Inference optimization
│
└── 14. Staying Sharp & Career
    ├── Reading papers fast (abstract, figures, evals)
    ├── Testing new models on your own evals, not on launch charts
    ├── Writing up what failed and why
    ├── Portfolio: 3 deep projects > 15 tutorial clones
    ├── Interviews: AI system design, eval design, debugging a broken agent
    └── Shipping something real users touch

    ◆ CHECKPOINT 100: you can design, build, evaluate and post-train AI systems

items.title: Military-made AI tool helped thwart World Cup bomb threat - Federal News Network
items.summary:
A military-made artificial intelligence tool helped law enforcement thwart a bomb threat at the FIFA World Cup in California this summer.

The previously undisclosed incident occurred June 18, when Switzerland faced Bosnia and Herzegovina at SoFi Stadium outside Los Angeles, Army Capt. Ryan Hetrick, who leads the Pentagon’s Generative AI Task Force, said Nov. 6 at an AI event in Washington. [...] Hetrick pointed to a recent visit to the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, where he built an AI tool that cut the time it takes to execute a particular cyber operations workflow from 100 hours to 15. That tool is now available to all cyber officers across the department, he said.

“We don’t do policy shops. We don’t do PowerPoints. We go to the edge and build with the warfighter,” he said. “You can’t be building agents from the Pentagon.” [...] He urged others across the military to adopt his hands-on approach to AI integration, encouraging troops to partner with AI experts to learn cutting-edge techniques and to tap innovative service members as in-house AI gurus who can spread that knowledge further.

        Sign up for our daily newsletter so you never miss a beat on all things federal

items.title: Công nghệ lượng tử đặt an ninh thông tin, dữ liệu trước nguy cơ mới
items.summary:
Công nghệ lượng tử là lĩnh vực khai thác các trạng thái và hiện tượng đặc biệt của vật chất, ánh sáng ở cấp độ nguyên tử để thu thập, xử lý và truyền tải thông tin với độ chính xác cao. Ba trụ cột chính của công nghệ này gồm: Tính toán lượng tử, truyền thông lượng tử và cảm biến lượng tử. [...] Công nghệ lượng tử đang được nhiều quốc gia xác định là lĩnh vực có ý nghĩa chiến lược đối với chủ quyền số, an ninh quốc gia và năng lực cạnh tranh. Các chính phủ và tập đoàn lớn đẩy mạnh đầu tư, xy dựng hệ sinh thái nghiên cứu, phát triển công nghệ, đồng thời tăng cường kiểm soát xuất khẩu thiết bị, vật liệu và phần mềm liên quan.

  
 Phòng nghiên cứu của Đại học Quốc gia Thành phố Hồ Chí Minh. Ảnh: TTXVN [...] Đến năm 2030, Việt Nam hướng tới xy dựng chiến lược quốc gia về công nghệ lượng tử, hoàn thiện cơ chế chính sách thúc đẩy phát triển lĩnh vực này; rà soát toàn bộ các hệ thống trọng yếu và xy dựng lộ trình chuyển đổi sang mật mã hậu lượng tử.

Việc cử cán bộ đi học không chỉ nhằm bổ sung văn bằng mà hướng đến trang bị kiến thức, kỹ năng để trực tiếp tham mưu, triển khai và giải quyết những vấn đề thực tiễn về công nghệ thông tin, chuyển đổi số tại cơ sở. [...] Đối với các học viên, đồng chí đề nghị xác định rõ trách nhiệm học tập, phát huy tinh thần chủ động, cầu thị; gắn kiến thức được đào tạo với những vấn đề thực tiễn đang đặt ra tại cơ quan, đơn vị. Mỗi học viên cần phấn đấu không chỉ sử dụng thành thạo công nghệ mà còn có khả năng tham mưu, đề xuất giải pháp, hướng dẫn đồng nghiệp, trở thành lực lượng nòng cốt thúc đẩy chuyển đổi số tại địa phương.

items.title: Terence Tao says that the AI proof on the Navier–Stokes problem is correct, yet mathematicians learned almost nothing fr
items.summary:
Terence Tao says that the AI proof on the Navier–Stokes problem is correct, yet mathematicians learned almost nothing from it. The proof is 100 pages, AI-generated and full of issues in its text, but a formal certificate in the language Lean confirms it.

Navier–Stokes is a Millennium Prize problem that asks whether the equations for fluids like water can start smooth and then blow up, with velocity or pressure becoming infinite. Human mathematicians came very close, and OpenAI ran its biggest model, with millions of dollars of compute, to get there first.

A human proof normally comes with talks on what was tried, what worked and what it connects to, like picking fruit and planting the seeds. Tao calls this one strip mining: the fruit taken, the landscape left barren. One colleague, using lots of AI, could explain only half of it after days of work.

items.title: Recent advances in AI are creating a 'paradigm shift' for robotics - Berkeley News
items.summary:
Traditionally, engineers can directly program the software that tells robots how to perceive objects, plan movements and control their actions, a process called model-based robotics. Or, with model-free robotics, they can train robots to learn behaviors from demonstrations through imitation learning. The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] Berkeley-based Ambi Robotics, which specializes in logistics and warehouse order fulfillment, applied the new methods earlier this year to analyze parcel sorting data and test updates to robot behavior. Tests showed an increased capacity of over 15,000 packages sorted annually per robot; the change is now deployed across 30% of the company’s U.S. fleet. [...] Ken Goldberg

“Agentic robotics is a fundamental shift in how robots are controlled,” Goldberg said. “Instead of collecting massive amounts of data and hand-tuning every behavior, teams of agents can quickly generate, test and refine robot programs that allow human engineers to interpret how the programs work for fine-tuning and verification.”

items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: Anthropic and OpenAI are coming for the development workflow | InfoWorld
items.summary: This is clearly where the frontier labs are moving, even though they’ve all benefited from an industry that provided neutral spaces to build. For example, OpenAI developed Pando, a Git back end for its own monorepo, to handle more engineers and agents reading and writing code concurrently. Its engineers kept using Git. OpenAI retained compatibility with the protocol and client and contributed improvements upstream. That compatibility let it rebuild the back end around the way its engineers [...] This pressure to maximize profitability helps explain why frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are aggressively adding functionality to own more of the developer’s workflow. On November 4, OpenAI announced an agreement to buy Pierre, the company behind Code Storage and the open source libraries Codex already uses to browse files and review changes. OpenAI wants Codex to be where developers work, from the first branch an agent creates through deployment of the application. There’s money in [...] OpenAI or Anthropic could build the place developers prefer to work. The question is what happens when a team likes that place and wants a rival’s agent for a particular job. Maybe a startup has built a tool that can track down the intermittent test failure that’s had the team stumped for a week. Give it access to the code and test history the team has authorized, and it gets a chance to prove itself. Ask the team to move its work to a new platform first, and it probably never gets to try.
